source: Peabody, Improving Planning: Quantitative Evaluation of the Premortem Technique in Field and Laboratory Settings (Michigan Tech master's thesis), Exp 1
finding: Field test with Army cadets. Teams that used the premortem to check their own plans had fewer fouls and less fixation than teams using the standard military plan check. Planning and execution time did not change.
numbers: Exp 1: 52 Army Cadets in teams, six time-constrained field exercises, 3 with premortem and 3 with standard military plan evaluation. Fouls and fixation lower with premortem. Test statistics not on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only; the full PDF was blocked (HTTP 403 and a bot check), so effect sizes and the fixation scoring are unknown. Master's thesis, not peer reviewed. Thesis year is not shown on the page I read (2022 is a guess).
agent_relevance: A rare outcome-based test (fouls in a real task) in a military-style setting. It supports using a failure frame on short horizons at no time cost. Not a test of an LLM.

source: Peabody thesis, Exp 2: Premortem versus Worst-Case Scenario Method
finding: When individuals judged their group's engineering plan, the premortem and the worst-case method gave no significant difference in the number of reasons and solutions. They did differ in which categories the reasons fell into.
numbers: Exp 2: 72 individual participants from university organizations; number of reasons and solutions not significantly different; category distributions significantly different.
limits: Abstract only. This is a null result on the headline count against a close rival that also imagines failure, but is not a hindsight frame.
agent_relevance: Rival frames find equally many causes. The value of a failure frame may be in steering which causes appear, not how many. Our agent can pick the frame by the kind of fault it needs to find.

source: Peabody thesis, Exp 3: Premortem versus Worst-Case Scenario, groups versus individuals, complex unfamiliar plan
finding: With a complex, unfamiliar plan, the premortem produced more reasons than the worst-case method. Groups produced more solutions than individuals. Reason categories again differed by method.
numbers: Exp 3: 82 participants, face to face. Premortem > worst-case on number of reasons; groups > individuals on solutions. Effect sizes not given on the page.
limits: Abstract only. Together with Exp 2 this suggests the premortem advantage over a worst-case frame depends on the task (complex and unfamiliar helped; the engineering plan did not). No outcome check of reason quality is stated.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the failure frame helps most when the plan is unfamiliar and complex. A cheap premortem pass is most justified at the impasse state, not on easy items.

source: Kannan (2026) Designing with Foresight: Premortem and Human-Centered Evaluation of Emerging Technologies (Michigan Tech dissertation, Exp 3 and 4)
finding: The premortem was more effective than other reasoning techniques for evaluating plan confidence. A Structured Premortem built for plans that use AI was then tested in a smaller experiment.
numbers: Exp 3: n=138 individuals and n=30 in groups. Exp 4: n=41 (Structured Premortem for AI plans). No means or effect sizes on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; PDF blocked (403). 'More effective' is stated for confidence, which is a belief measure and not plan quality. Dissertation, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Newest human test, with a structured version for AI-based plans. Watch for the full text: it may say what structure helped. Confidence shift is still the measured outcome.

source: Jason Collins' review page on premortem evidence: Veinott, Klein and Wiggins (2010) PreMortem versus other methods
finding: Students judged a university's H1N1 lockdown plan. Imagining the plan had failed cut confidence about twice as much as pros-and-cons or cons-only. After solutions were generated, confidence rose most in the premortem condition.
numbers: N=178, five conditions. Roughly 2x the confidence drop of the comparison methods. No test statistics on the page.
limits: Secondary page. Outcome is confidence, not whether the plan was better. Students and a hypothetical plan. Conference paper, no direct replication shown. The page says the literature is thin.
agent_relevance: Supports using a failure frame as a trigger that lowers false confidence. The rise in confidence after fixes is a possible stop signal, but only if a code check backs it.

source: Same page: Gallop and Bischoff (2016) premortem versus brainstorming with experienced managers
finding: Experienced program managers and engineers, in teams, found more quality risks, made more effective plan changes, and found more black-swan risks missed in a historical case with a premortem than with brainstorming.
numbers: N=101 in teams of 4-6; 45 minutes; torpedo fuse scenario; blind expert panel; quality = score above 70 on both dimensions. Exact counts and effect sizes not given in the text.
limits: Secondary page; the figure with counts was not visible. One scenario. The comparison is to brainstorming, which does not impose a failure frame, so it cannot separate the frame from simply being told to look for faults.
agent_relevance: Best expert-panel evidence that the frame adds quality. Still no test that the risks found were real.

source: Same page: what the Mitchell et al. (1989) number does and does not show
finding: The 30% is an increase in the number of reasons generated when an event is imagined as already done. Reason quality was not assessed. Klein (2007) restated it as 30% better at correctly identifying reasons, which the paper did not measure.
numbers: About 30% more reasons (Mitchell, Russo, Pennington 1989). Exact N and test not on the page.
limits: Secondary source. Primary paper not read this session.
agent_relevance: Do not count cause volume as accuracy. Our agent should rank generated causes by whether code can confirm them.

source: Implementation Science Communications (2025) Proactive planning for contextual fit: the role of the implementation premortem
finding: A 2025 review repeats the claim that prospective hindsight raises the ability to correctly identify failure explanations by 30%, citing Mitchell 1989, and says it significantly reduces overconfidence, citing a search-and-rescue study (Hill 2012). This shows the overstated version is now standard in the literature.
numbers: Claim: +30% (Mitchell 1989); reduced overconfidence (Hill 2012). Its reference list also names later work to chase: Roose, Lehman, Veinott 2023 (game teams); Zhang et al. 2024 (future-oriented perspective and wise reasoning); Park, Lu, Hedgcock 2017 (forward vs backward planning); Meissner and Wulf 2015.
quote: Prospective hindsight has been found to increase the ability to correctly identify potential explanations for program failure by 30%
limits: Review, no new data. I read the text and the reference list only; I did not open the cited studies. The 30% wording conflicts with the finding that quality was not measured.
agent_relevance: Citation drift is a warning for our own notes: mark the 30% as 'more reasons', not 'better reasons'.

source: Gilmartin et al. (2019) Brainwriting Premortem: a novel focus group method to engage stakeholders
finding: Ten brainwriting premortem sessions with 116 health staff produced many barriers quickly. The authors say the premortem has never been formally evaluated and ran no head-to-head comparison.
numbers: 116 staff in 10 sessions (2 to 26 each). 364 ideas, 217 unique, 93 agreed, 15 expanded. Brainwriting took about 10 minutes; whole session 60-90 minutes. Surveys after only 6 of 10 sessions (73% response).
limits: No control condition. Quality of ideas judged by three coders, subjectively. Text says unique ideas ranged up to 100 per site but the table shows 39: the source is inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Shows a written, parallel, no-discussion version is cheap and productive. For us: independent samples written without seeing each other, then merged by code, is the analogue.

source: Beidas et al. (2022) Promises and pitfalls in implementation science: learning from a pre-mortem (Implementation Science 17:55)
finding: Ten mid-career researchers imagined that implementation science had failed and produced six themes by consensus. The article gives no evidence that the exercise improved outcomes and cites only Mitchell 1989 for the idea.
numbers: N=10; 6 themes (e.g. recreating the research-to-practice gap; overly complex strategies).
limits: Applied exercise, no control. Only the first 100,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Typical of current use: the premortem is applied widely and tested rarely.

source: Wippold et al. (2024) Application of an implementation premortem using prospective hindsight (Transl Behav Med)
finding: Qualitative premortem with Black men on a barbershop health program. Participants were told the program had failed and gave reasons. The article credits prospective hindsight with a 30% gain, citing only Mitchell 1989, and does not test the method.
numbers: N=23 (mean age 40.45, SD 14.62); 35-60 minute groups; 5 minutes of silent writing; top coded priorities: Implementation Phase 166, Outer Context 132, Program Fit 110 mentions.
limits: No comparison condition, not preregistered, data on request only. Authors note the facilitator's verbatim script may have seemed cold, so delivery can matter.
agent_relevance: Evidence of use, not of effect. Note that framing wording and delivery were a stated risk.

source: Student poster, SJDM 2020: premortem versus promortem and brainstorming on confidence (reported in a search snippet)
finding: A snippet of this poster says that in its first experiment people who reasoned forward about success ('promortem') were more confident than people who reasoned backward from failure ('premortem'). In the second experiment there were no statistical differences.
numbers: Exp 1 differences in confidence by direction; Exp 2 null. No N or statistics seen.
limits: I did not open the poster (connection refused). Only a search-result summary, student poster, not peer reviewed. Treat as a lead to verify.
agent_relevance: If the second experiment is null, the confidence-drop effect is not robust. Candidate failed replication to check.

source: Koellinger and Treffers (2015) Joy leads to overconfidence, and a simple countermeasure (PLoS ONE)
finding: Reviewing debiasing, the authors say they could find no empirical evidence that the premortem works against overconfidence, though it could dampen optimism in principle. Their own working countermeasure was making people reflect on their mood and whether its cause was relevant.
numbers: No premortem data. Their effect: a joyful mood induction raised overconfidence; reflecting on mood and its irrelevance restored calibration.
quote: Although we could not find empirical evidence that this debiasing strategy works, it may in principle dampen excessive optimism.
limits: A 2015 statement. Later studies (2019-2026 theses above) are small and mostly unreviewed.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping the premortem as a tested option, not a trusted rule. The mood result hints at a rival: the cheap, specific 'is this cue relevant?' question.

source: Wikipedia: Hindsight bias, debiasing section
finding: The page says counterfactual prompting reduced hindsight bias and that thinking how alternative hypotheses could be right was the one observable way to cut it. It does not mention Mitchell's prospective hindsight. No method removes the bias.
numbers: No effect sizes for debiasing. Bias itself: 75% of failed entrepreneurs predicted success vs 58% recalled the prior belief (Hoelzl et al. 2002). Faster answering raised the bias (Calvillo 2013).
limits: Encyclopedia summary, no numbers for the fixes; original studies (Arkes et al. 1988, Fischhoff 1975) not opened. Only the first 100,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Rival to the premortem: 'consider the opposite' or explain alternatives. The premortem is one member of that family, so its effect should be compared with the plainer 'give a reason you could be wrong' prompt.

source: arXiv 2610.02740 (2026) Prospective Hindsight: Self-Calibrating Reinforcement Learning via Prediction-Reality Gaps
finding: A name collision, not a premortem. It is an RL training signal: the agent predicts its own outcome before feedback, and samples where prediction and result differ most get higher gradient weight. It says it improves task performance and calibration across scales under GRPO.
numbers: Abstract has no figures. Tested on single-turn verifiable tasks and a multi-turn personal-agent task.
limits: Abstract page only. It is training, which we do not do. It does not cite Mitchell or the premortem.
agent_relevance: Related idea we can use without training: log the agent's own confidence before a check, and treat the gap with the check result as the surprise signal that triggers deeper thinking.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking the model to review its own answer made accuracy worse or no better. With the correct label used to decide whether to revise, it looked much better, which is why earlier papers looked positive.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after one self-correction round, 41.8 after two. GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, GPT-4 HotpotQA 49 -> 59.
limits: Tests a generic 'review your answer' prompt, not a premortem. 100 HotpotQA questions in places; models from 2023.
agent_relevance: Our G1/G2: an unprompted 'imagine it failed' without a code-found failing output is probably this same intrinsic self-critique and may lower accuracy. Pair any failure frame with a real check.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models were poor at finding which step of a reasoning chain was wrong, but good at fixing it once told the step. So the weak part of self-critique is finding the fault, not repairing it.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 chains over 5 tasks. Best model (GPT-4) reached 52.87 overall mistake-finding accuracy on direct step prompting. A small trained classifier beat prompting large models at locating errors.
limits: Tasks are algorithmic and the traces are skewed to few mistakes; text notes that gains depend on starting accuracy (50% -> 68.6% vs 99% -> 92.8%).
agent_relevance: A premortem makes the model imagine faults; this says the model is bad at locating real ones. Locating the fault should be done by code (G2), and the model asked only to repair.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) Self-reflection in LLM agents: effects on problem-solving performance
finding: Nine LLMs re-answered questions they got wrong after producing reflections. All eight reflection types beat the baseline (p < 0.001). Even 'Retry', which only says the first answer was wrong, helped across all models.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 8 reflection types, multiple-choice exams; every reflection type significant at p < 0.001. Types with more information (Instructions, Explanation, Solution, Composite) beat limited ones (Retry, Keywords, Advice).
quote: even the mere knowledge that the agent previously made a mistake improves the agent's performance
limits: Only questions the model got wrong are re-asked, and the model is told it was wrong: that is outside information about failure. Authors note possible leak of the answer through the reflection and ceiling effects at over 90% accuracy.
agent_relevance: Shows that a known-failure signal is itself useful. This supports an impasse trigger from code (we know the answer failed) over self-generated doubt.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: After a failed attempt, the agent writes a verbal lesson into memory and tries again. Gains over baselines were large, but the failure signal came from the environment or unit tests.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%; roughly +22% on AlfWorld, +20% on HotPotQA, +11% on HumanEval over baselines.
limits: Relies on a trustworthy failure signal (tests, environment reward). Huang 2024 notes this oracle dependence. Not a prospective failure frame: failure has actually happened.
agent_relevance: A real post-mortem works when failure is real. A premortem is the case where it has not happened, and the evidence is weaker.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction
finding: Survey conclusion: no prior work shows successful self-correction from feedback by a prompted LLM, except in tasks unusually suited to it. Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists, and large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Three findings: (1) no clear success with prompted-LLM feedback; (2) works with reliable external feedback; (3) works after large fine-tuning. Many studies over-evaluate through unfair setups.
limits: Survey; I read only the abstract and introduction.
agent_relevance: Adds weight to the rule that a failure frame must be paired with code-based feedback. A pure prompt premortem is in the category with no demonstrated gain.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse thinking makes LLMs stronger reasoners (RevThink)
finding: A reasoning variant that goes backward from the answer. Student models trained on forward and backward reasoning did better, and the backward check acts as a consistency test.
numbers: 12 datasets; average +13.53% over zero-shot student; +6.84% over best distillation baseline; 10% of data beat standard fine-tuning on 10x forward data.
limits: Requires training with teacher-made backward data, not a prompt-only change. Backward here means from solution to question, not from imagined failure to causes.
agent_relevance: Backward thinking has an AI result, but by training. A prompt-time version is a consistency check by code, such as checking an answer against the question.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Built a taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three groups from 150 traces, then scaled to 1600+ traces. LLM-as-judge annotation agreed with humans at kappa 0.77. Failure rates on seven open multi-agent systems ranged from 41% to 86.7%.
numbers: 150 traces to build; 1600+ annotated; 14 modes; human agreement kappa 0.88 in final rounds; LLM annotator kappa 0.77; failure rates 41% to 86.7% on 7 systems.
limits: Describes failures after the fact, not predicted in advance. Taxonomy of existing frameworks, may not match a single agent.
agent_relevance: A list of real failure modes could seed a code-held premortem checklist, so failure scenarios come from data and not from model imagination.

source: Who&When (2025) Which agent causes task failures and when? Automated failure attribution
finding: Asked LLMs to name which agent and which step caused a failure in logged runs. The best method found the agent 53.5% of the time but the step only 14.2%. Some methods were below random. Strong reasoning models were still not practical.
numbers: 127 multi-agent systems logged; best 53.5% agent-level, 14.2% step-level accuracy; o1 and R1 did not reach practical usability.
limits: Explaining real failures from logs, a post-mortem not a premortem. Dataset of agent systems from 2024-25. Author list not recorded.
agent_relevance: If models cannot reliably explain a failure that has happened, explaining a failure that has not happened is likely weaker. Cheap fault location by tests should come first.

source: Gap: full text of Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989), Veinott et al. (2010), Hill (2012), Park et al. (2017) not obtained
finding: These are the key studies for the effect size and mechanism. Hill (2012, search-and-rescue planners) is cited for reduced overconfidence; Park, Lu, Hedgcock (2017) compare forward and backward planning. I could not open them.
numbers: No numbers verified. Only the Mitchell '+30% more reasons' appears second hand.
limits: Paywalls, bot checks and a shared search budget stopped me. Of 6 allowed searches, 2 were used and the second was refused by the tool.
agent_relevance: Do not cite effect sizes from these in the schema until the primaries are read.

source: Gap: no LLM study of a premortem was found in 2020-2026
finding: Crossref searches for premortem or pre-mortem with language model, agent or prompting returned no study that tests a premortem prompt on an LLM. arXiv title searches were mostly rate limited, so this is not a complete search.
numbers: Crossref: 4 phrasings, 12 results each, none testing a premortem prompt. The only AI paper with the name was the RL 'Prospective Hindsight' paper found through arXiv.
limits: Absence of evidence from a partial search. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate limited; arXiv API returned 429 most times.
agent_relevance: Treat any gain from a premortem prompt on our agent as untested and measure it with our own A/B (plain vs failure frame vs code-found failure).

source: Design implication, not a source: code-supplied failure scenario versus model-imagined failure
finding: Putting the human results next to the LLM results: people gain from a failure frame mostly by losing false confidence and by listing more reasons; LLMs lose accuracy when asked to doubt without a failing output, and gain when a real failing signal exists. So the failure scenario should come from code.
numbers: Combines Huang 2024 (75.8 -> 38.1 on CommonSenseQA) and Renze 2024 (Retry alone helps) with the human count-versus-quality gap.
limits: My synthesis, not a measured result. No experiment tests the combination.
agent_relevance: Candidate test: arm A plain; arm B 'imagine this failed and list causes'; arm C code finds a failing check, then the model explains it. Predict C > A >= B on accuracy.
